title: Equivalent Fractions by Multiplying
short: Multiply top and bottom by the same number: the pieces get smaller, the amount stays.
trouble: Children add the same number to the top and bottom, thinking 2/3 equals 4/5.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you saw with pictures that 1/2 and 2/4 name the same amount. Now you will see why, and get a rule that works for any fraction.

Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number, and you get an equivalent fraction: $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 4} = \dfrac{8}{12}$. The pieces get smaller, there are more of them, and the amount stays the same.

Start with $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of a bar: 2 of 3 equal pieces are shaded. Now cut every piece into 4 smaller pieces. The bar has $3 \times 4 = 12$ pieces, and the shaded part has $2 \times 4 = 8$ of them. Nothing was added or taken away; you only cut. So $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{12}$. Multiplying the bottom by 4 makes the pieces 4 times smaller; multiplying the top by 4 counts 4 times as many of them. The two changes cancel out.

blocks.name: fractionbar
blocks.cap: Use Cut each part into to cut $\dfrac{2}{3}$ into smaller pieces: $\dfrac{4}{6}$, $\dfrac{6}{9}$, $\dfrac{8}{12}$. The shaded length never changes.

blocks.name: fractioncircle
blocks.cap: The same idea with a circle: cut each fourth in two and $\dfrac{3}{4}$ becomes $\dfrac{6}{8}$.

blocks.title: Find a missing numerator
steps: The denominator went from 5 to 20: it was multiplied by 4.

blocks.title: Test a claim
steps: $\dfrac{4}{5}$ comes from adding 2 to the top and to the bottom, not multiplying.
Compare with the same denominator: $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{10}{15}$ and $\dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{12}{15}$.

blocks.name: fractionbar
blocks.cap: Adding the same number to the top and bottom changes the amount: $\dfrac{4}{5}$ is longer than $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

blocks.html: Adding the same number to the top and bottom, thinking $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{5}$. Adding does not cut pieces evenly, so the amount changes. Only multiplying (or dividing) both by the same number keeps it the same.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4, 4.NF.A.1 (explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to (n × a)/(n × b) using visual fraction models)
